sentences.text: Chindesaurus was a bipedal carnivore roughly the size of a wolf, with estimates of its length ranging from 2 to 4 meters and its weight between 23 and 45 kilograms.

Its skeleton featured deep, wide, and short trunk vertebrae resembling herrerasaurids, neural spines that expanded outward to form 'spine-tables,' a thin pubis bone curved backward, and a large femur with a smooth, rectangular head.

The most complete specimen, known as PEFO 10395, includes a single tooth, fragmentary neck and back vertebrae, rib fragments, two complete hip vertebrae, and a complete left femur, while the type and paratype specimens measured approximately 2 to 2.3 meters in length.

The genus name Chindesaurus combines the Navajo word chindi, meaning 'ghost' or 'evil spirit,' with the Greek word sauros, meaning 'lizard,' a combination that has long been opposed by Native American consultants due to its association with a taboo concept.
Neural spines in Chindesaurus expanded outward and backward to form 'spine-tables,' a unique structure also found in the genera Herrerasaurus and Dilophosaurus.
The holotype specimen was discovered in 1984 by Bryan Small in a blue mudstone layer near Chinde Point in Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, where it was initially thought to be a prosauropod.
The holotype, nicknamed 'Gertie,' was airlifted by helicopter on June 6, 1985, to the University of California Museum of Paleontology for preparation.
Chindesaurus was formally described and named by R.A. Long and P.A. Murry in 1995, who classified it as a herrerasaurid and chose the specific name bryansmalli to honor the discoverer.
The ancient floodplain environment where Chindesaurus lived also contained abundant lungfish and clams.

Research suggested that the Chindesaurus and Tawa clade belonged to basal Saurischia, before the split between sauropodomorphs and theropods, leading to its classification within the family Herrerasauridae and as a herrerasaurid theropod.

A 2019 study suggested Chindesaurus was a theropod closely related to Tawa, while a 2026 study placed it in a new clade called Morphoraptora, grouping it with Tawa as non-herrerasaurid herrerasaurians based on a unique trait: a posterior margin on the proximal tibia divided by two notches.
A partial ilium originally assigned to Chindesaurus was later classified as a separate species, Caseosaurus crosbyensis, by Hunt et al. in 1998.

Chindesaurus lived in the southwestern United States during the Late Triassic, approximately 213 to 210 million years ago, with the fossil record spanning from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago during the Norian stage.

Langer (2004) argued that Caseosaurus and Chindesaurus likely represent the same species rather than distinct genera, a view supported by Nesbitt et al. (2007) who suggested differences were due to size-related variation. However, because both species are so fragmentary, researchers decided not to formally make them synonyms, though Nesbitt, Irmis, and Parker noted that the affinities of Chindesaurus cannot be fully verified due to the great similarity of preserved parts with Saturnalia and the absence of much of the skeleton.
